Course roadmap

The two sessions move in a single continuous arc: light enters the eye, is refracted onto the retina, is converted into a neural signal, and that signal travels a defined path to the cortex — a path clinicians can interrogate piece by piece at the bedside.

From optics to neural processing — the original lecture slide.
The journey of sight in five stages: refraction → translation (phototransduction) → automation (autonomic control) → transmission (the pathway) → diagnostics (bedside exam).

Big pictureThe entire discipline of neuro-ophthalmic localization rests on one idea: the pattern of visual field loss is a coordinate map of where the lesion sits. Learn the pathway once, and every visual field defect becomes readable.

Learning objectives

  • Trace the path of light from cornea to retina and name the four refracting surfaces.
  • Explain the retina's "inverted wiring" and contrast rods vs. cones.
  • Describe autonomic control of pupil size and lens shape, and the near triad.
  • Trace the full visual pathway from retina to occipital cortex, and explain why the optic nerve is classified as a CNS tract.
  • Perform and interpret the four-part bedside optic nerve exam.
  • List causes of optic neuropathy.
  • Localize a lesion along the visual pathway from a visual field defect.
1 · Refraction

From light to image: the optics of the eye

Vision begins with refraction — light bending as it crosses surfaces of different optical density.

Why light bends

Light refracts whenever it crosses a boundary between media of different optical density. The first refraction happens immediately, at the air–cornea interface, because air and the cornea differ in optical density.

The eye works, collectively, as a single convex lens system built from four convex refracting surfaces in series:

Cornea→ Aqueous humor→ Lens→ Vitreous humor→ Retina
  • Cornea — the transparent anterior convex surface; contributes most of the eye's refractive power.
  • Aqueous humor — fluid in the anterior chamber; second refracting surface.
  • Lens — the only refractive element that can change shape (see Accommodation, next tab).
  • Vitreous humor — fills the posterior chamber; final refraction before the image lands on the retina.
High yield ⭐⭐Four convex surfaces, in order: Cornea → Aqueous humor → Lens → Vitreous humor.
The optical pathway: four convex refracting surfaces bring light to a focus on the retina.

Refractive errors

Normal image formation vs. astigmatism, myopia, and hyperopia.
ConditionWhat happensCorrection
AstigmatismIrregular curvature scatters light so it does not converge to a single point on the retina.Cylindrical lens to correct the irregular curvature.
Myopia (near-sighted)Eye is relatively too long/big — the image forms in front of the retina.Concave lens, to diverge light before it enters the eye.
Hyperopia (far-sighted)Eye is relatively too short/small — the image forms behind the retina.Convex lens, to converge light more strongly.
Clinical pearlMyopia = image falls in front of the retina → correct with a concave lens. Hyperopia = image falls behind the retina → correct with a convex lens.
2 · Retina & phototransduction

The retina: an inverted, layered transducer

Once light reaches the retina it must be converted into a signal the brain can use — and, paradoxically, it must first pass through the retina's neural layers to reach the actual sensors.

Energy conversion cascade

Light energy→ Chemical energy→ Electrical energy→ Transmission to brain

The main factor driving the light→chemical conversion step is Vitamin A.

High yield ⭐⭐⭐Vitamin A is the key factor converting light energy to chemical energy in photoreceptors. Vitamin A deficiency impairs night vision (poor adaptation to low-light / scotopic conditions) — think of this whenever a patient reports nyctalopia (night blindness).
The retina's reverse wiring — light must cross the ganglion and bipolar layers before reaching the photoreceptors.

Reverse neural wiring

Because the retina is inverted, the order encountered by incoming light is the opposite of the order signals travel to exit the eye:

Layer (light path, outer→inner)Cell typeRole
Inner layer (outermost relative to light)Ganglion cells — 2nd order neuronAxons converge to form the optic nerve.
Middle layerBipolar cells — 1st order neuronRelay between photoreceptors and ganglion cells.
Outer layer (innermost relative to light)Photoreceptors (rods & cones)Convert light into chemical, then electrical signals.

After phototransduction, the resulting electrical impulses travel in the opposite direction to incoming light, back through the retinal layers, to the nerve fibers that form the optic nerve.

Rods vs. cones

Photoreceptor specialization: rods for night vision, cones for daylight, acuity, and color.
FeatureRodsCones
Vision typeNight vision — ScotopicDaylight vision — Photopic
SensitivityHighly sensitive — function even in dim lightLess sensitive — need brighter light
LocationPeriphery of the retinaConcentrated in the center; the very center of the macula (fovea) contains cones only
Visual acuityNot responsible for acuityResponsible for visual acuity
Color perceptionNo role in colorResponsible for color perception
High yield ⭐⭐⭐Cones alone occupy the very center of the retina (fovea/macula) — this is why central fixation gives the sharpest, most colorful image, and why Snellen acuity testing is really testing cone/macular function.
3 · Autonomic control of the eye

Adapting to light and distance

The eye continuously self-adjusts along two independent autonomic axes: how much light enters (pupil), and how strongly light is bent for near objects (lens/accommodation).

Pupil size — adapting to light intensity

Two intrinsic (internal) muscles inside the iris control pupil diameter — distinct from the extrinsic (external) recti/oblique muscles that move the globe.

  • Constrictor pupillae — circular muscle; contraction narrows the pupil. Supplied by the parasympathetic system, traveling with the oculomotor nerve (CN III) to the ciliary ganglion.
  • Dilator pupillae — radial muscle; contraction widens the pupil. Supplied by the sympathetic system.

Bright light → pupil constricts (smaller). Dim light → pupil dilates (larger).

Dynamic aperture — parasympathetic constriction vs. sympathetic dilation.

The pupillary light reflex

Afferent (sensory) limb in blue, efferent (motor) limb in red.
Bilateral midbrain projection explains why light in one eye constricts both pupils.
  • Afferent limb: retina (ganglion cell fibers) → optic nerve → optic chiasma. These pupillary fibers actually leave the optic tract before reaching the lateral geniculate body and instead project to the midbrain.
  • They synapse at the pretectal nucleus, which projects bilaterally to both Edinger-Westphal nuclei.
  • Efferent limb: Edinger-Westphal nucleus → oculomotor nerve (CN III), both sides → ciliary ganglion → constrictor pupillae.
High yield ⭐⭐⭐Because roughly half the optic nerve fibers decussate at the chiasma, and the pretectal nucleus projects to both Edinger-Westphal nuclei, shining light in one eye constricts both pupils: a direct response in the illuminated eye and a consensual (indirect) response in the other. The direct response is normally stronger than the consensual response.
Clinical pearlLocalizing a sluggish/absent pupillary reflex: if the pupil reacts, but weakly, suspect an optic nerve (afferent) problem. If the pupil is fixed and dilated, not reacting at all, suspect an oculomotor nerve (efferent) problem.

Accommodation — adapting to distance

Rays from a distant object arrive essentially parallel (as if from infinity), so little refractive effort is needed. Rays from a near object are divergent, so the eye must work harder to bring them to a focus — this extra work is accommodation, performed by the lens.

  • The ciliary muscle is attached near the iris and, via the suspensory ligaments (zonules), controls lens shape.
  • For near vision, the ciliary muscle contracts, the suspensory ligaments relax, and the lens — naturally elastic — becomes rounder/more convex.
  • For distance vision, the ciliary muscle relaxes, ligament tension increases, and the lens flattens.
Clinical pearl — PresbyopiaBy around age 40, the lens loses elasticity and the eye progressively loses the ability to accommodate for near objects — presbyopia, corrected with reading glasses.

The near triad

The near triad — a single synchronized, autonomically-mediated response to viewing a near object.

1

Miosis

Pupil constricts, sharpening the image (like closing a camera aperture).

2

Accommodation

Lens rounds up via ciliary muscle contraction.

3

Convergence

Both eyes turn inward so the divergent near-object rays still land on corresponding retinal points.

High yield ⭐⭐Convergence is produced by bilateral contraction of the medial recti. The near triad (miosis + accommodation + convergence) is entirely controlled by the autonomic nervous system.
4 · Visual pathway

From retina to occipital cortex

One continuous relay carries the visual signal from each eye to the primary visual cortex — the anatomical backbone for every localization question below.

The visual pathway: retina → optic nerve → chiasma → tract → LGB → radiation → cortex.
Retina→ Optic nerve→ Optic chiasma→ Optic tract→ Lateral geniculate body (thalamus)→ Optic radiation→ Occipital (visual) cortex
  • The optic nerve begins at the retina and ends at the optic chiasma.
  • At the chiasma, fibers from the nasal retina of each eye decussate (cross), while temporal-retina fibers stay uncrossed — this is why each optic tract carries information from the same half of the visual field for both eyes.
  • Past the chiasma, the pathway continues as the optic tract, ending at the lateral geniculate body (LGB) — part of the thalamus, and the third-order relay for this sensory pathway.
  • From the LGB the fibers fan out as the optic radiation, splitting into two bundles that run alongside two different lobes before reconverging: one runs near the temporal lobe, the other near the parietal lobe.
  • Both bundles terminate in the occipital cortex — the primary visual area is Area 17, with additional supporting visual areas nearby and in other lobes.
Nasal retinal fibers cross at the chiasm; the left brain ultimately sees the right visual field, and vice versa.

Why is it called the optic "nerve" — or should it be a "tract"?

For every other sensory modality in the body, the first-order neuron is peripheral, the second-order neuron sits in the CNS (e.g. spinal cord), and only after that second synapse does the pathway become a true CNS "tract." In vision, the second-order neurons (the retinal ganglion cells) already sit inside the eye — functionally equivalent to the spinal cord being pulled all the way forward into the globe. Because there is no further synapse between the retina and the lateral geniculate body, the entire optic nerve is, strictly, a CNS tract that only looks like a peripheral nerve. Its myelin sheath (oligodendrocyte-type, CNS myelin) differs from that of true peripheral nerves as well.

High yield ⭐⭐⭐The optic nerve is a CNS tract, not a true peripheral nerve, because its second-order neurons (retinal ganglion cells) lie inside the retina itself — there is no additional synapse between the retina and the lateral geniculate body.
The optic nerve's two pathways from its origin in the retinal ganglion cells: the primary (vision) pathway synapsing at the LGB, and the secondary (reflex) pathway bypassing it to reach the pretectal nuclei in the midbrain.
5 · Bedside assessment

Clinically testing the optic nerve

Every neurological work-up pairs a functional assessment with a structural one. For the optic nerve, that means four functional tests plus one structural test.

Every clinical test isolates a specific anatomical structure along the visual pathway.

Functional test 1

Visual acuity

Formal fixed-distance test of the fovea/macula and cone function, most commonly using the Snellen chart. The patient fixates centrally; this isolates the sharpest point of vision.

Functional test 2

Visual field

Tests the function of the rest of the retina while the eye stays still (any eye movement converts the test back into acuity testing). Formally via a visual field (perimetry) machine; at the bedside via the confrontation test.

Functional test 3

Color vision

Uses pseudoisochromatic plates, most classically the Ishihara chart. Defects can be congenital/developmental (commonly red or green) or acquired — acquired color-vision loss raises concern for optic nerve pathology.

Functional test 4

Pupillary light reflex

Assesses the integrity of the afferent (CN II) and efferent (CN III) limbs of the reflex arc described in the previous tab.

Snellen chart (acuity) and visual field mapping.
Ishihara plates test cone integrity / color perception.

Structural test: Fundoscopy

The optic nerve is the only nerve in the body that can be directly visualized — along with the retinal blood vessels — via an ophthalmoscope. Key landmarks:

  • Optic nerve head (disc) — exit point of ganglion cell axons; the "blind spot."
  • Macula — area of central vision.
  • Fovea — the very center of the macula, containing cones exclusively; the point of peak acuity.

A parasympatholytic eye drop is often used first to block the constrictor pupillae and dilate the pupil, widening the viewing angle through the round pupillary aperture.

Fundoscopy: the window to the CNS.
How to perform the confrontation test (step by step) High yield
  1. Examiner and patient sit facing each other, at the same eye level.
  2. Each covers one eye (patient's covered eye is opposite the examiner's covered eye).
  3. The patient fixates on the examiner's open eye without moving their own eyes — any eye movement converts the test into an acuity test rather than a field test.
  4. The examiner brings a target (finger/pen) in from the periphery in each of the four quadrants — temporal, inferior, nasal, superior — and the patient reports as soon as it becomes visible.
  5. Because the examiner has (presumed) normal fields, the patient's field is compared quadrant-by-quadrant against the examiner's own.
  6. Repeat with the other eye.

Blind spot vs. scotoma

Left: normal physiologic blind spot. Right: an abnormal central scotoma superimposed on it.

Every normal eye has a physiologic blind spot corresponding to the optic disc, which contains no photoreceptors. It normally goes unnoticed because the visual system adapts to it and the two eyes' visual fields overlap. A scotoma is a pathological field defect indicating optic nerve or macular dysfunction.

Summary — four-point examVisual acuity (Snellen) · Visual field (confrontation/perimetry) · Color vision (Ishihara) · Pupillary light reflex — plus structural fundoscopy.
6 · Optic neuropathy

Causes of optic nerve dysfunction

An overview of etiologic categories (detailed disease-specific work-up belongs to internal medicine/neurology courses).

Afferent (sensory) vs. efferent (motor) failure isolates the neural circuit involved.
Etiologic categories of optic neuropathy.
CategoryExamples
Infectious / parainfectiousViral infections; post-viral immunization reactions
ToxicSmoking (tobacco), alcohol, drugs such as ethambutol (patients on ethambutol require optic nerve monitoring)
Demyelinating (most important)Immune system targets the myelin sheath — e.g. optic neuritis in multiple sclerosis
Systemic autoimmuneSLE, sarcoidosis
TraumaTraumatic optic neuropathy
CompressionMass effect from a tumor
High yield ⭐⭐Demyelination is highlighted as the single most important cause of optic nerve dysfunction to remember at this level.
Typical presentation pattern of optic nerve dysfunction: reduced acuity, RAPD, dyschromatopsia, central/paracentral field loss.
7 · Localization atlas

Reading the visual field: lesion localization

Companion reference figures: the same pathway from tab 4, now read in reverse — starting from a visual field defect and walking back to the lesion site.

Core principleA visual field defect is not just a pattern on a page — it is a precise coordinate map of the pathology's location along the pathway.
1 · Optic nerve lesion

Defect: complete monocular (unilateral) blindness in the affected eye.

Key sign: relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD, "Marcus Gunn pupil") in that eye.

Clinical pathology tags: optic neuritis (demyelination), ischemic optic neuropathy, compressive lesions.

The swinging flashlight test: the diagnostic bedside sign for a relative afferent pupillary defect.
2 · Optic chiasm lesion

Defect: bitemporal hemianopia — loss of the temporal (outer) visual field in both eyes, because it is the crossing nasal retinal fibers (which carry the temporal visual field) that are compressed. Classic etiologies: pituitary adenoma, craniopharyngioma, anterior communicating artery aneurysm. High-yield pearl: an anterior chiasmal syndrome can create a junctional scotoma — ipsilateral central blackout with a contralateral superior temporal defect.

3 · Optic tract lesion

Defect: contralateral homonymous hemianopia. The incongruity rule: because fibers here are less tightly organized than more posteriorly, tract lesions often produce jagged, mismatched (incongruous) field defects. Key sign: RAPD may be present, since the optic tract is still proximal to the pupillary light reflex fibers exiting just before the LGB. Blood supply: anterior and posterior choroidal arteries.

4 · Optic radiation lesions

Note: lesions distal to the LGB do not produce an RAPD. Meyer's loop (temporal lobe): sweeps anteriorly into the temporal lobe; carries inferior fibers → contralateral superior quadrantanopia ("pie in the sky"); MCA territory, temporal lobectomy risk. Baum's loop (parietal lobe): passes directly through the parietal lobe; carries superior fibers → contralateral inferior quadrantanopia ("pie on the floor"); MCA territory.

5 · Visual (occipital) cortex lesion

Defect: contralateral congruous homonymous hemianopia — by the time fibers reach the cortex they are perfectly aligned, so defects are perfectly symmetric between the two eyes. Macular sparing: the fovea has massive cortical representation with a dual blood supply (PCA + MCA collateral supply), so an isolated PCA infarct destroys peripheral vision but the MCA collateral keeps the central macula alive.

Anton-Babinski syndrome: bilateral occipital (cortical) blindness with denial of blindness and confabulation.

High-yield localization heuristics

Four rules that solve most localization questions.

Rule 1

The optic nerve rule

Pre-chiasmal lesions are strictly monocular.

Rule 2

The chiasm rule

Chiasmal lesions are bitemporal.

Rule 3

The retrochiasmal rule

Post-chiasmal lesions are homonymous (affecting the same side of both eyes' fields).

Rule 4

The congruity rule

The further posterior the lesion, the more congruous the defect (Tract → incongruous; Cortex → congruous).

"Follow the wire, find the cut": a visual field defect is a precise coordinate map of the lesion.
Other reference figures from this atlas

An altitudinal defect (loss of upper or lower half of field in one eye) — typically ischemic optic neuropathy or branch retinal vessel occlusion.

Diagnostic synthesis: anterior lesions present monocularly; chiasmal lesions present bitemporally; post-chiasmal lesions present homonymously.

One-page exam-cram summary

Physiology

  • 4 convex surfaces: cornea → aqueous → lens → vitreous
  • Myopia = image in front of retina → concave lens
  • Hyperopia = image behind retina → convex lens
  • Retina: ganglion (2°) → bipolar (1°) → photoreceptors
  • Vitamin A: light → chemical energy; deficiency → night blindness
  • Rods: scotopic, peripheral, sensitive, no acuity/color
  • Cones: photopic, central/macular, acuity + color
  • Constrictor pupillae: parasympathetic, CN III
  • Dilator pupillae: sympathetic
  • Near triad: miosis + accommodation + convergence
  • Convergence: bilateral medial recti
  • Presbyopia: accommodation loss ~age 40

Pathway & clinic

  • Retina → optic nerve → chiasma → tract → LGB (thalamus) → radiation → occipital cortex (Area 17)
  • Optic nerve = CNS tract (2° neuron already in the retina)
  • Pupillary reflex: afferent CN II, efferent CN III, relay midbrain (pretectal → bilateral Edinger-Westphal)
  • 4-part optic nerve exam: acuity, field, color, pupillary reflex + fundoscopy
  • Optic nerve lesion → monocular defect ± RAPD
  • Chiasm lesion → bitemporal hemianopia
  • Tract lesion → incongruous homonymous hemianopia
  • Temporal radiation (Meyer's loop) → superior quadrantanopia
  • Parietal radiation (Baum's loop) → inferior quadrantanopia
  • Occipital cortex → congruous homonymous hemianopia ± macular sparing
